blocks.text: Striking with its feet its dear chattering wings: as though the locust spoke with its wings. But most to the point here is the verb κατακριδεύειν [katakrideuein], formed ἀπὸ τῶν ἀκρίδων [apo tōn akridōn], from locusts, which means to deafen someone with one's chatter, as if you were to say locustare [to locust]. Hesychius: Κατακριδεύσει· καταλήσει (read καταλαλήσει·) ἐπεὶ καὶ αἱ ἀκρίδες πολύφωνοί εἰσιν· [Katakrideusei; katalēsei (read katalalēsei;) epei kai hai akrides polyphōnoi eisin;] He will locust (if the word may be pardoned), he will overwhelm with chatter; for locusts are most loquacious. But, to return to the matter: when the Prophet says of the coming people of locusts, Before it fire shall consume, and behind it a flame shall burn, I think that in both places he is speaking of an extreme drought, which preceded and followed the arrival of the locusts. And therefore the Prophet says, Before it (the people of locusts) shall consume, etc. The land of Canaan is compared with the garden of Eden, as Egypt and the land of the Sodomites before the disaster sent by God, Gen. XIII, 10. Before it, that is, before its arrival; as behind it, that is, after its departure; as in Zachar. VII, 14. The land was desolate after them, that is, after their migration ^{(2)}.
And nothing shall escape it.] That is, of the produce of the land. For they will consume everything so that absolutely nothing is left.

Verse 4. Its appearance is like the appearance of horses, and like horsemen so shall they run] As in Apoc. IX, 7. And the shapes of the locusts were like horses prepared for battle. The Hebrews refer this to the speed of their running or flight, in which they are nearly equal to horses; we refer it in addition to the head or face, which is not unlike a horse's. From this the Italians call locusts cavallette. Hence Albertus, book 26: They have a head with the shape of a horse. And Aldrovandi: They have a head somewhat like a horse's. And long before, Theodoret on Joel: Εἴ τις ἀκριβῶς κατίδοι τὴν κεφαλὴν τὴν ἀκρίδος, σφόδρα τῇ τοῦ ἵππου [III, 308] ἐοικυῖαν εὑρήσει· [Ei tis akribōs katidoi tēn kephalēn tēn akridos, sphodra tē tou hippou eoikuian heurēsei;] If anyone considers the head of a locust attentively, he will find it very similar to the head of a horse. And Muhammiaddin Assarhuriensis, a poet of some renown among the Arabs:

لها فخذ ابكر وساقا نعامة [lahā fakhdh abkur wa-sāqā naʿāma] وقادمتا نسر وجوجو ضيغم [wa-qādimatā nasr wa-jūjū ḍayghama] ☼ ذنبها افاعي الارض وانعمت عليها [dhanabuhā afāʿī al-arḍ wa-anʿamat ʿalayhā] [col. 475] جياد الخيل بالراس والغم [jiyād al-khayl bi-l-rās wa-l-ghamm] ☼

They have the thigh of camels, the legs of an ostrich, the wings of an eagle, the breast of a lion. Their tail is like that of the vipers of the earth; and the noble horses have graced them with their form in head and mouth. And another anonymous Arab in Damiri: في جرادة خلق عشرة من جبابرة الحيوان مع ضعفها وجه فرس وعينا فيل وعنق ثور وقرنا ايل وصدر اسد وبطن عقرب وجناحا نسر وفخذا جمل ورجالا نعامة وذنب حية [fī jarāda khalq ʿashara min jabābirat al-ḥayawān maʿa ḍaʿfihā wajh faras wa-ʿaynā fīl wa-ʿunuq thawr wa-qarnā ayyil wa-ṣadr asad wa-baṭn ʿaqrab wa-janāḥā nasr wa-fakhdhā jamal wa-rijlā naʿāma wa-dhanab ḥayya] In the locust, weak as it is, is the nature of ten great animals: 1. the face of a horse, 2. the eyes of an elephant, 3. the neck of a bull, 4. the horns of a stag, 5. the breast of a lion, 6. the belly of a scorpion, 7. the wings of an eagle, 8. the thighs of a camel, 9. the feet of an ostrich, 10. the tail of a serpent. In this list the face of a horse is put first of all. For بطن عقرب [baṭn ʿaqrab] the belly of a scorpion, read بطن عقاب [baṭn ʿuqāb] the belly of a black eagle. For the scorpion, which is smaller than the locust, can have no place among those great animals. True, there follows وجناحا نسر [wa-janāḥā nasr] and the wings of an eagle. But عقاب [ʿuqāb] and نسر [nasr] are different species of eagles. Abarbanel anxiously inquires why the Assyrians, whom he holds Joel to be treating here, are compared with horses or horsemen. At one moment he understands by horses the Centaurs, whom the horsemen of the Chaldeans resembled; at another he contends that their foot soldiers were like real horses in stature, strength and speed. Everyone sees how absurd this is. Of Centaurs there is here neither trace nor track; nor would any sane person believe that the Chaldeans are said by the Prophet to be like an animal that exists nowhere. And for foot soldiers to be compared with horsemen is novel and unheard of. Finally, who would say that the Assyrians were like horsemen, when they really were horsemen, and in great numbers? Scripture teaches this expressly in Ezech. XXIII, 6. 12. 23. and XXVI, 7. 10. 11. Nahum. III, 2. Hab. I, 8. etc.
